title: Shark Attacks
text:
The Global Shark Attack File (GSAF), maintained by the Shark Research Institute, is a worldwide record of reported interactions between humans and sharks. Drawing on more than 5,000 cleaned incident reports from 1901 through 2018—including country, water activity, and outcome—this site examines where shark encounters occur and what actually happens when they do.
Movies and headlines often portray sharks as a constant threat to beachgoers, yet fear of sharks is vastly out of proportion to the real risk. Even with hundreds of millions of people entering the ocean every year, recorded shark bites remain rare, and roughly four out of five incidents with a known outcome are non-fatal. Ordinary coastal hazards such as rip currents pose a far greater danger to swimmers than sharks—while many shark species face severe population declines from human fishing.
Use the navigation bar above to explore the patterns in the data. The Map page displays reported shark attacks by country across the globe, showing how strongly incidents cluster along heavily used coastlines in the United States, Australia, and South Africa. The Trends page compares fatal and non-fatal attacks across the most common ocean activities, revealing why high-exposure sports like surfing see the most encounters overall even though swimming accounts for more fatalities.
